source.title: Symbolic Rule Extraction from Attention-Guided Sparse Representations in Vision Transformers

record.file_problem: None noted; the paper text and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines whether neurons in a vision model show selective or mixed visual-concept responses using attention heatmaps and semantic labeling, a different measurement from the original examples.
record.gate_note: The study visualizes three neurons for the P3.1 dataset and explicitly describes two as responding to mixed features and one as consistently activating for the bed concept. It does not measure the population share of mixed-selectivity neurons or establish that the mixed features are unrelated. Classification and rule-set metrics do not measure the claim's subject and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: In a new setting, a ViT-Base with an added sparse sigmoid concept layer, the authors inspect top-activating images and heatmaps for three neurons. They report two neurons respond to mixed features rather than one concept. The evidence is qualitative and incidental to the paper's main rule-extraction goal.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that NeSyViT beats vanilla ViT accuracy by 5.14% with compact rule-sets. They find semantic labelling unreliable in ViTs due to limited neuron monosemanticity, with some neurons responding to mixed features. They propose heatmap inspection as a partial remedy and improved monosemanticity as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a sparse concept layer with supervised contrastive, entropy, and L1 sparsity losses and inspects attention heatmaps; it does not reproduce the original neuron examples or their measurement method.
record.peer_reviewed: Theory and Practice of Logic Programming 25 (2025) 722-738
record.problems: The neuron evidence is qualitative and limited to three selected neurons from one dataset setting. The study does not report a population-level rate, quantify the mixed responses, or show that the mixed features are unrelated. The stated uncertainty values concern other reported metrics, not these neuron observations.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and Table 2 classification-accuracy and rule-set metrics were left out because they do not measure neuron response selectivity. The Appendix B rule listings are not separate reported measurements of attention-map responses.

untested.parts: InceptionV1 and its canonical examples are not studied. The paper gives no share of polysemantic neurons and no evidence that the mixed features are unrelated.
No test of superposition as a cause.
No test of initialization, regularization or noise as causes.
There is no comparison of architectures or losses on the polysemantic share. ViT versus CNN labelling reliability is asserted, not measured.
Does not analyse whether the mixed responses reflect one shared feature.
No comparison of activation ranges or scoring methods.

missing.what: Conclusion states automatic labelling struggles in ViTs due to 'limited neuron monosemanticity'. This is a general qualitative claim with no count.

record.verdict_notes: The record's limits_scope label from r1 is dropped: a single monosemantic neuron does not qualify V1, which claims only that some neurons are polysemantic. The inspected neurons belong to a layer trained with L1 sparsity, entropy and supervised contrastive losses. Several labelled predicates in the appendix combine related scene objects, e.g. kitchen items. Those labels come from IoU labelling, not a test of relatedness, so they are not used for V6.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55, the cat-face/car-front example, or how common mixed responses are across neurons.
No language models, tokens, or language-model neuron response rates are studied.
Does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity in networks with sufficient capacity.

Uses a sparse concept layer and combined losses, but does not compare architectures or training conditions for their effect on the share of polysemantic neurons, or quantify a performance tradeoff for reducing that share.
Does not determine whether the mixed responses share a feature or are related offshoots of one job.
Does not compare activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods to show how measurement choices affect polysemanticity.

relation.reason: The authors' own inspection of neuron heatmaps (Fig. 2a) reports two neurons responding to mixed features. This bears on V1, though weakly and incidentally.

tranche.reason: The study is not aimed at the polysemanticity question, so it is not T2. It is a new setting (ViT-Base with an added sparse concept layer) with an incidental qualitative result on V1, which is T3.

source_check.notes: The evidence is one qualitative sentence (Fig. 2a) about 2 of the 3 rule-set neurons in an added 128-unit sigmoid layer. That layer is trained with SupCon so neurons specialise by class, which means the mixtures may be parts of the same scene rather than unrelated inputs. The P3.1 rule-set labels in Fig. 2b differ from the P3.1 rule-set in Appendix A.

statements.correction: Neurons 43 and 105 are 2 of the 3 rule-set neurons for P3.1, in a 128-unit sparse concept layer. They show no clear concept selectivity and respond to mixed features. Neuron 106 activates consistently for bed in bedroom images (Fig. 2a).
statements.problem: Accurate for this study. Minor nuance: the three neurons in Fig. 2a are all the predicates of the P3.1 rule-set. Only the dataset was picked for display, not the units. Neuron 106, the third, is clearly selective (bed).

statements.correction: The units are outputs of an added sparse concept layer (128 units, sigmoid) fed by the [CLS] token. They are not native backbone MLP neurons.
statements.problem: Correct: the neurons are units of a 128-dim sigmoid linear layer that replaces the ViT-Base classification head. It is trained on top of ImageNet-1k pretrained weights.

statements.correction: arXiv:2505.06745 (r2, r3): the mixed features are not named or shown to be unrelated. The layer is trained with a supervised contrastive loss so that neurons fire mainly for one class.
statements.problem: Nothing it says about this study is wrong. However, it cites r2 without naming arXiv:2505.06745 in the issue text.
